title: fly.pieter.com
tagline: The vibe-coded MMO flight sim that started the craze: built live on X, sold in-world ads, hit a self-reported $87k MRR in 17 days.

creator.name: Pieter Levels
creator.background: Dutch solo indie hacker (Photo AI, Nomad List) with ~600k X followers; had never made a game before

summary: A free, instant-load browser flight sim billed as an MMO: you pick a free Cessna 172, the free 'Cyberpink' craft or a paid $29.99 F-16 and fly over a city of skyscrapers with other players. You can shoot balloons, collapse buildings and dogfight, and later updates added Mars and space flight. Startups' ads float in the world as blimps and branded objects.
highlights: Widely cited as the first vibe-coded game to go massively viral: 1.58M views on the launch post, a repost from Elon Musk, and a reader-estimated 100M+ views across the whole saga
Built from a one-line Cursor prompt, entirely in public on X, adding features in response to replies
Ads are part of the world (blimps, branded objects), so the game works like a 3D billboard; the first non-tech sponsor signed by 10 March 2025
Real-time multiplayer dogfighting with no loading screens or installs, and it also runs on mobile
Its playbook (ship fast, build in public, sell in-world sponsorships) was copied within days by games like VibeSail, and it led to the Vibe Jam
story:
Pieter Levels started the game on 22 February 2025 by typing 'Make a 3d flying game in browser with skyscrapers' into Cursor, and built most of it live on X. A first version took about three hours (404 Media and others repeat a '30 minutes' figure for the initial build). Over the next days he added shootable balloons, collapsing buildings, mobile support and multiplayer. He struggled to make hits register, so he had Grok 3 write a WebSocket server, with X users chipping in. He added Mars after Elon Musk, who had reposted the game, replied.

He monetized it like a 3D Million Dollar Homepage. Startups including bolt.new, CodeRabbit and Synthflow bought in-world ads, and the F-16 sold as a paid upgrade. He reported $67k MRR on day 13 (6 March 2025) and $87k MRR ('$1M ARR') on day 17, and went on to host the 2025 Vibe Coding Game Jam. Revenue later faded. A December 2025 blog estimate put it at about $5k/month, and a 2026 write-up says his X bio reads 'Pieter.com $0/m'. Both are secondary sources, and the bio line may refer to pieter.com as a whole. The game is still online, and its homepage links to a DroneSim spin-off, a live flight radar and merch.

vibeCoding.aiCodeShare: ~100% (the site says '100% made with AI'; self-reported)
vibeCoding.buildTime: first version in ~3 hours on 2025-02-22; updated live for weeks afterwards
workflow: Opening prompt in Cursor: 'Make a 3d flying game in browser with skyscrapers'; vanilla HTML/JS plus Three.js
Built in public on X and shipped what replies asked for (shootable balloons, collapsing buildings, mobile, Mars)
Used Grok 3 to write the WebSocket multiplayer server after struggling to make hits count and dogfights work; X users helped
Used ChatGPT to find and remove duplicated features and code
Tried Claude 3.5 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet inside Cursor; Levels said AI made it '10-100 times' faster than coding it by hand

art.notes: Rendered in Three.js from AI-written code, with no loading screens and the site's claim of '100% made with AI'. Sources don't say whether any aircraft use imported models, so treat 'code-generated' as inferred.

tech.notes: Vanilla HTML/JS front end with Three.js, which matches Levels' usual no-framework style. Real-time multiplayer runs on a WebSocket server written with Grok 3. The levels.io post URL slug ('full-multiplayer-python-websockets-game-ai') suggests a Python websockets backend, but the post text doesn't confirm it. One report says the server peaked near 2,000 simultaneous players.

traction.monetization: Free to play. Revenue came from in-world ads sold to startups (blimps, branded objects; sponsors on 6 March 2025 included bolt.new, Synthflow, CodeRabbit and Scaledropship), a $29.99 F-16 upgrade and merch. Ad prices are reported inconsistently: '$5,000/month' (Niche Site Growth, March 2025), 'blimps at $1,000/week' (Snyk), and one blimp sold for $1,000.
traction.notes: The numbers conflict. 404 Media's lede says '$50,000 a month' while its body says 'thousands of dollars a month'. Snyk claims '$100K+ MRR at peak', which Levels' own $87k figure doesn't support. Peak concurrency is variously given as ~2,000 on the server, 17,000 and 26,000, and '31,000' was a daily total that others turned into a concurrent figure. The ads didn't renew, so revenue decayed after the viral spike.

reception: It became the poster child of vibe coding. Elon Musk reposted it, it got massive reach, and copycat ad-funded browser games followed within days. Skeptics, starting with 404 Media's 'Yours Probably Won't', credited Levels' huge audience rather than the code, and developer Max Yankov said making it work well for many players would take '100-1000 times more effort'. Indie Hackers reported that his sites were hit by DDoS attacks after the game went viral.
lessons: Distribution did the heavy lifting: a ~600k-follower audience plus a Musk repost sold the ads, and creators without an audience rarely matched it
Sponsorships and one-time purchases are not recurring revenue; MRR fell sharply once ad slots lapsed and the novelty faded
Going viral brings attackers: his sites were DDoSed. Specific cheating incidents weren't confirmed in this research pass
Multiplayer hit registration was the hard part even with AI, and it needed a dedicated WebSocket server
Charge from day one, while attention is at its peak

title: Battle Drones
tagline: A Command & Conquer-style mobile web RTS built by Claude over 321 commits, with audio-modem multiplayer and LLM-vs-LLM battles.

creator.name: Simon Willison
creator.background: veteran web developer (Django co-creator, Datasette) and prolific LLM blogger; describes his own game-dev experience as limited

summary: A browser RTS in the mold of Command & Conquer and Red Alert that runs on phones and desktops. You harvest scrap, build a base and fight with ground, air and infantry drones under fog of war, where air and ground targets need different weapons. Modes include symmetric Skirmish, Last Stand survival waves, an 8-mission Ops campaign, a Daily Op, a seeded random map generator and rule-bending mutators. There is also a Goliath mech that can anchor to found a new base. You can fight six AI commander personalities, duel friends over sound or the internet, or watch LLMs play each other.
highlights: Audio-modem local multiplayer: two devices within microphone range sync game state through sound, so no server is needed. Claude first built a 'Radio Probe' tool to measure the acoustic channel's bandwidth.
Claude balanced the game by running 1,200+ AI-vs-AI matches. Stalemates still undecided after 25 minutes fell from 14% to 0.9%, and wins by a side 800+ scrap behind rose from 24% to 46%.

Six AI commander personalities (Balanced, Rush, Air Swarm, Boom, Skyforce, Ironclad) at three difficulty levels. An Agent-vs-Agent mode lets LLMs such as GPT-6 Luna, Gemini 4 Argon and Claude Haiku 5.5 play each other through tools that only show what each side can see, with every match recorded as a replay.
Fully deterministic simulation for replays and multiplayer. Claude even replaced Math.sin and Math.cos with custom versions because browsers returned slightly different results.
Claude modeled every 3D unit and building in TypeScript/three.js code, and an in-game model browser shows them off. The soundtrack is synthesized in code and intensifies as battles heat up.
Mutators like 'Robot Love', where Goliath mechs that get close fall in love and the game ends in a draw.
story:
Simon Willison wanted an RTS he could play on his phone that recaptured the 1995 Command & Conquer and Red Alert. He started in July 2026 with Claude Fable 5. That first version was 2D Phaser with AI-generated sprites and, in his words, 'wasn't great to play'. From v3 onward he used Claude Opus 5.5 through Claude Code, Claude Code for Web and the subagent-orchestrating 'Ultracode' mode. Over 12 major versions, with 321 commits at launch mostly by coding agents, he barely looked at the code. He playtested it himself and steered with prompts like 'This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun.' (v4) and 'Port this game to three.js with 3D models for all of the buildings and vehicles and landscapes' (v5).

He launched it publicly on 20 October 2026. Online multiplayer over a tiny WebSocket relay followed the same week, and a four-player 'Compass Rose' map arrived on 24 October from a single prompt. A steampunk fork, Panache by Gabriel Turpin, appeared the day after launch. In his follow-up 'vibe game development' post, Simon called it his most successful game project. He said none of his game projects took more than four hours of his own work, plus a lot of background agent time.

vibeCoding.aiCodeShare: ~100% (Simon says he reviewed almost none of the code, the commits are mostly by coding agents, and Claude even wrote the README)
vibeCoding.buildTime: July to October 2026: 12 major versions and 321 commits by the launch post (346 on main by Nov 2026). Under about 4 hours of Simon's own work, plus long, sometimes overnight, agent runs.
workflow: Started with 'Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions' and grew the game one big version at a time.
Vague quality prompts worked: 'This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun.' produced the v4 'Fun Update'.
Design-first prompts for big features, e.g. a long Archipelago map spec ending 'First research and then critique this design. Only build after we have agreed on any modifications'.
Time-boxed creative prompts. The random map generator came from '...You have 45 minutes to build this! Be creative.'
Claude Code 'Ultracode' dynamic workflows coordinated many subagents on complex changes. Simon says it 'burns tokens like there's no tomorrow'.
Claude built its own tools: a Radio Probe bandwidth tester, a replay viewer, and an llm plugin (llm-tools-battledrones) that lets LLMs play.
Simon gave Claude an OpenAI API key so it could generate sprites and textures and look at the results itself.
Testing used 1,200+ simulated AI-vs-AI matches, Vitest unit tests, Playwright smoke tests and Simon's own playtesting.

art.style: 3D drones, mechs and buildings modeled in three.js code over AI-painted terrain; began as 2D AI sprites
art.notes: v1 and v2 used 2D sprites from OpenAI image models. Claude wrote the image prompts, looked at the results and iterated. For v3, Opus regenerated the sprites and made background tiles for five new maps. From v5, Claude built every model in TypeScript with three.js, with team colors red, blue, purple and green. The README says terrain, menu art and icons were painted with OpenAI's gpt-image-2.5-sunburst through an art pipeline that calls the Images API.

audio.notes: The project ships no audio files. Music varies by map and intensifies as battles heat up. Unit voices and an announcer are also listed, and the README says all sound is synthesized live in the browser. The high-pitched audio-modem tones used for local multiplayer gave Simon's partner a headache, so a warning was added (PR #36).

tech.notes: Began in Phaser (2D) and was ported to three.js/WebGL in v5. It is a static site on GitHub Pages and an offline-capable PWA (Simon played it on a plane). Local multiplayer is an over-the-air audio modem using the microphone. It grew out of his Chirp Pong experiment, with ggwave and Siner as prior art. For online play, WebRTC attempts failed even on the same Wi-Fi network. Claude instead wrote a stateless asyncio Python WebSocket relay on Fly.io (shared-cpu-1x, scale-to-zero, estimated at no more than $2.19/month) that pairs browsers by room code via share link or QR code. Up to four humans can play on Compass Rose, with AI filling any empty slots. The deterministic sim, with custom trig in src/sim/fmath.ts, enables JSON replays.

traction.monetization: None: free and open source (Apache 2.0) on static hosting. The relay server is estimated at no more than $2.19/month.
traction.notes: No player counts published. It spawned at least one notable fork the day after launch: Panache by Gabriel Turpin, a steampunk Belle Époque reimagining with new music.

reception: Covered as a showcase of agent-built games, e.g. AI Weekly's 'Simon Willison ships vibe-coded RTS in 321 agent commits'. Simon says it convinced him Opus 5.5 understands what makes a game fun. He is still ambivalent: he admits to 'guilt' about building software this way. On the Steam 'no AI filter' debate, he says the game is 'still way too low effort' to count as a legitimate indie project, and he won't enter vibe-coded games in traditional jams. No Hacker News thread about the game itself was found. The HN link in his post is the Steam no-AI-filter thread.
lessons: Strategy games are unusually easy for bots to playtest: AI-vs-AI simulation gave the agent hard balance numbers (stalemate rate, comeback rate) to optimize.
Replays and multiplayer depend on determinism, all the way down to tiny cross-browser differences in floating-point trig functions.
WebRTC P2P was a dead end even on a single Wi-Fi network. A simple stateless WebSocket relay was cheap and reliable.
Model generation matters: the Fable 5-era 2D version 'wasn't great to play', and Opus 5.5 made it fun.
'Tools are effectively free': let the agent build its own measurement and debugging tools.
Agents miss human factors: the audio-modem tones caused headaches and needed a warning.

title: Claude of Duty
tagline: A three-paragraph prompt plus a swarm of Claude Opus 5 agents produced a ~55k-line, zero-asset, CoD-style FPS in Three.js.

extraLinks.label: Operation Blackout (playable rerun of the same prompt)

creator.name: Matt Shumer
creator.background: AI investor and former HyperWrite CEO; not a game developer

summary: A single-player browser FPS set on a ~120x120 m market street with enterable interiors and several hundred props. You fight skinned AI soldiers that use navmesh pathing, perception and cover, and ragdoll when they die. Movement and gunplay copy Call of Duty: sprint, slide, mantle, lean, ADS, spring recoil, procedural reloads and bullets with travel time and drop. Every texture, mesh, animation and sound is generated from code when the game loads.
highlights: Zero external assets: no models, HDRIs, image files or audio files. It has 19 procedural GPU surfaces with parallax occlusion and triplanar mapping, procedural weapon geometry, skinned soldiers and synthesized audio, all built at load time.

An AAA-style WebGL2 pipeline: HDR, cascaded shadow maps with PCSS, GTAO, TAA, motion blur, bloom pyramid, GPU exposure metering and AgX tonemapping. On top of that it has atmospheric scattering, time of day, volumetric fog and light shafts.
Physics written from scratch with no library: a SAH BVH (29k triangles into 14k nodes in 22 ms, 0.25 us per raycast), a character controller, rigid bodies, PBD ragdolls and bullet penetration.
The agents built their own QA tools: deterministic screenshot capture, image diffs, a profiler and scripted playtests. ARCHITECTURE.md served as the contract between the 11 subsystem agents.
A brutally honest self-assessment in the README: 11 adversarial critics scored frames 3.59 -> 4.14 -> 4.05 -> 5.05 out of 10 and picked real Call of Duty in every blind round.
It set off a wave of playable copycats: Dust Corridor (Leon Lin, Cursor + Opus 5) and Operation Blackout (James Altucher, same prompt, ~10 hours).
story:
Matt Shumer posted a demo on X on 2026-07-25, about two days after Claude Opus 5 launched, claiming 'Claude Opus 5 one-shotted this game' with 'not a single external art asset'. He published the MIT-licensed repo the same day, with the whole prompt in prompt.md. The prompt is three short paragraphs. It asks for a shooter 'at the level of the most recent Call of Duty games' and tells the model to 'fan out sub-agents', to '/loop' on every item, and to use a separate 'really harsh critic' sub-agent that compares the result blind against real Call of Duty. It ends with 'Do this in ThreeJS ... Fan out sub-agents and ultracode.' The run used Claude Code's Ultracode mode (top reasoning effort, up to 16 agents at once) and the /loop skill. It went on for hours until Shumer stopped the session himself. Shumer later called the structure the 'Gauntlet Loop'.

The README is unusually candid. It says the goal was to match a modern Call of Duty and 'It does not': critic scores rose only from 3.59 to 5.05 out of 10, and in blind A/B tests every critic picked the real game. Copycats followed within days. James Altucher ran the same prompt in Claude Code ultracode for about ten hours (~1.3M tokens according to Decrypt) and got Operation Blackout (operation-blackout-green.vercel.app). Leon Lin (@LexnLin) instead wrote a detailed ~20-section spec and used plain Opus 5 on high effort in Cursor to build Dust Corridor, a playable market-street tactical FPS (claude-of-duty-six.vercel.app). Rich of Atom Tan Studio reran the prompt on OpenAI's Sol 5.6 Ultra.

vibeCoding.aiCodeShare: ~100% (README: 'written by a fleet of AI agents under orchestration' from a single prompt)
vibeCoding.buildTime: one unattended Claude Code session that ran for hours (exact length not published); repo created and pushed 2026-07-25
workflow: A single 163-word prompt (prompt.md) asked for CoD-level quality, sub-agents per item, /loop on each item, and a harsh-critic sub-agent doing blind side-by-side comparisons with real Call of Duty.

Claude Code Ultracode mode: the model writes its own orchestration plan and spreads work across up to 16 agents at once (capped at 1,000 per run, per Decrypt). The /loop skill drove repeated fix-test-adjust cycles.
ARCHITECTURE.md defined the subsystem interfaces the agents worked against (render, materials, sky, world, physics, player, weapons, fx, ai, ui, audio).
Eleven adversarial critic agents scored captured frames out of 10 and labelled shots AMATEUR or CLOSE. The builder never graded its own work.

Logged finding: three rounds of six parallel agents, each owning a directory, gained only +0.46, and defects went 60 -> 47 -> 66. One sequential pass with a single owner per coupled concern gained +1.00 and cut defects from 66 to 26.

Reproducible capture: rendering each screenshot in a fresh page made output bit-identical. Shader pre-warm removed 34-35 in-game shader compiles, and imagediff.mjs confirmed the optimizations changed nothing visually.

art.notes: Everything is generated at load: procedural texture forge (19 surfaces such as concrete, brick and rusted metal), procedural guns, skinned soldiers and instanced props. The triangle count rose from 5.9M to 11.3M during the art passes. Weaknesses the README admits: hands, material richness up close, mannequin-like enemies at a distance and approximated indirect light. The viewmodel light rig gives about 20x the world's irradiance, which is still unfixed.

audio.notes: Synthesized in Web Audio with layered weapon fire, convolution reverb, HRTF spatialisation and occlusion. No audio files.

tech.notes: Three.js r180 is the only runtime dependency (dev dependencies: Vite, Playwright, pngjs). Performance at 1512x982 DPR 2 on the 'ultra' preset on an Apple silicon laptop: p50 went from 12-17 to 28-30 fps, the worst frame from 728-1236 ms to 66-82 ms and boot from 9-12 s to 3.7-4.6 s. Line count: the README says ~55k and BestHub says ~70k. A researcher count of the public repo on 2026-11-24 found ~66.9k raw lines in src/ (~69.6k with tools/), ~62k non-blank and ~49k without comment lines. Both figures are plausible depending on how you count. The game is not hosted; run it locally with npm run dev.

metrics.label: GitHub stars in first five days

traction.monetization: None (MIT-licensed open source)
traction.notes: No hosted build from the author. The hosted copycats are Dust Corridor (https://claude-of-duty-six.vercel.app/) and Operation Blackout (https://operation-blackout-green.vercel.app/).

reception: It went viral as the showcase for Opus 5 and agentic coding; Enterprise DNA called it 'the go-to proof point for one-shot agentic coding'. Skeptics disputed 'one-shot' because it took hours of looping with critics and sub-agents, and some suspected hidden manual coding. Shumer answered by publishing the prompt and the code. explainx argued both sides are right: it was one human prompt, but many model passes. Decrypt pointed out that FPS boilerplate (pointer-lock controls, WASD, raycasting) is all over public code, so 'data contamination' can't be ruled out, and none of the builds checked for it. Decrypt also noted that the copycats never faced Shumer's blind test.
lessons: Parallel agents that each own a directory break each other's assumptions in coupled systems such as lighting and materials. A single owner per coupled concern did twice as well.
Median frame rate hid the real problem: a benchmark showed 94 fps while gameplay was unplayable. Track p99 and worst-frame times.
Make visual QA reproducible before trusting AI critics: shared pages made 10 of 11 shots differ between runs.
An agent that contradicted its brief was right. The weapon was specular-dominated, not untextured, and needed higher albedo. Over-specified briefs can be wrong.
'One-shot' meant one human prompt, not one model pass. Even after hours of looping, the result scored about 5/10 against real Call of Duty.

title: A Game About Capybaras Delivering Food
tagline: An iOS dev's first game, built with Claude Code in ~2 weeks, took the $25k top prize at Cursor Vibe Jam 2026.

creator.name: Leo (leocoout)
creator.background: iOS engineer with ~9 years of mobile experience; this was his first game

summary: A cozy open-world delivery game. You are a capybara courier on a scooter: you take orders from an in-game phone app, buy the items at a minimart and race them to customers. Everything you carry stacks into a wobbling tower that tilts in turns and topples if you drift or speed. It has a single-player mode and an online mode where everyone shares one city.
highlights: Carried food stacks into a physics tower that tilts in turns and can topple. He deliberately made it less realistic so it stays fun
Claude built a parody iPhone UI in CSS in one pass: slide-to-unlock, notification badges, and spoof apps 'CapyMaps' and 'Capify'

Claude built him in-game tools: a level editor (terrain sculpting, surface painting, model placement), a road tool that turns control points into asphalt with sidewalks, lamps, guardrails and markings, and a timeline cutscene editor
Online players who were in the city while he recorded the intro cutscene appear in the opening animation
Everyone shares one global city over a Cloudflare WebSocket. Position, carried food, chat, horn honks and nearby players' music are synced
PS1-inspired look (low-res textures, limited palettes, reduced resolution) on a deliberately mixed map with Christ the Redeemer, the Golden Gate Bridge and the Hollywood Sign
story:
Leo (@leocooout) is an iOS engineer with nearly nine years of mobile experience, and this is his first game. He made it for Cursor Vibe Jam 2026 in about two weeks (his write-up says '15 days') and submitted it on April 29, 2026. He spent week one getting the core loop working before any visual polish. Most of his time went to brainstorming, planning and playtesting, while Claude Code (Opus 4.7) wrote the code: over 27,000 lines in 188+ commits. Partway through he paid an extra $100 to move from the Claude Code Max 5x plan to Max 20x.

On June 17, 2026 Pieter Levels named it the #1 game of 945 entries ($25,000). Levels described it as a capybara delivery driver in Rio de Janeiro who takes orders on a delivery app, buys them at a 7/11 minimart and drives to customers. In July Leo posted a detailed breakdown on r/vibecoding and Medium. Wccftech, Mac Observer, 36Kr, IT Home and AIbase covered it, mostly framing it as 'one person and Claude Code beat 900+ entries for under $150.'

vibeCoding.aiCodeShare: ~100% (creator says the game was 'entirely vibe-coded'; Claude wrote the code while he did the 'thinking')
vibeCoding.buildTime: ~2 weeks (15 days) in April 2026; submitted 2026-04-29
workflow: Ran 2–3 Claude Code sessions in parallel, each owning one module (map, UI, physics), so they didn't edit the same code
Started a fresh session with no prior context for each new feature, and kept one long-running session for bugs that needed accumulated context
Built a sandbox test map and a debug panel to tune driving, drifting, collision, camera and boost
When the AI couldn't do something directly (generate a whole city), he had it build tools instead: level, road and cutscene editors
Got the core gameplay fun in week one before any art polish
Brainstormed gameplay, art style and characters with GPT and Grok before generating assets

art.notes: Characters were designed with GPT and Grok, then turned into 3D models with Tripo3D Pro ($19.9/mo). Giving Tripo front, back, left and right views of each character made much better models. GPT Images 2 (free trial) made the logo, illustrations and textures (asphalt, grass, dirt, wood, sand, water, farmland), and Claude swapped them into the map's flat-color areas. 2D billboard trees replaced placeholder trees. Asking AI to generate the whole city failed: building placement was hard to control, detail dropped up close, and one big map was hard to optimize. So Leo placed the map by hand in the editor Claude built, which he called the most labor-intensive part. Roads and their props are generated procedurally from control points.

audio.notes: Background music from Suno and sound effects from ElevenLabs, both on free tiers.

tech.notes: Three.js client. Multiplayer is one global city/lobby on a live Cloudflare WebSocket service that relays player positions, item stacks, chat, honks and music. Leo says a ~5-player room works fine but server load rises a lot with dozens of players, so the design doesn't suit large-scale games. Wccftech quotes him: 'Multiplayer was simpler than expected for a jam.' The jam listing marks it mobile-ready.

traction.monetization: None. Free web game (jam rule); earned the $25,000 prize.
traction.notes: No player counts published. Sources differ on cost (AIbase: +$100 plan upgrade; 36Kr: under $150 total) and timeline (two weeks vs. 15 days). AIbase's '188 submissions' figure appears to confuse the 188 commits with the entry count; the official count is 945.

reception: Levels called it 'a super cute game' when naming it the #1 winner. Leo's July write-up spread widely in tech press (Wccftech, Mac Observer, 36Kr, IT Home, AIbase). The Wccftech author doubted a layperson could reproduce it and framed Claude Code as a productivity boost for skilled developers. Leo himself stressed this is not a 'one prompt makes a game' story; 36Kr's headline takeaway was 'the greatest value of AI is not writing code.'
lessons: AI couldn't produce a usable 3D city. Having AI build editors and placing the level by hand worked
Use fresh sessions for new features and one persistent session for debugging
Parallel agents need clear module boundaries to avoid conflicts
Realism isn't fun: physics were tuned for entertainment, not accuracy
A simple WebSocket relay is enough for a jam but doesn't scale beyond small rooms
The human's job was design, planning and playtesting; Claude 'was responsible for writing code'

title: World of ClaudeCraft
tagline: Open-source WoW-style browser MMO whose foundation Claude built in a weekend, now with 9 classes, a 10-player raid and an RL agent mode.

creator.name: Levy Street Games
creator.background: Wellington, New Zealand AI company (CEO Max Polaczuk, lead developer Reuben Horne); the CEO had used classic MMOs as a reinforcement-learning research testbed

summary: A free, classic-era (vanilla-WoW-like) MMORPG that runs in desktop and mobile browsers. You pick one of nine classes (each with three talent specs) and quest through zones like Eastbrook Vale and Mirefen Marsh. There are 5-player dungeons, delves, ranked arenas, 5v5 capture the flag and a 10-player raid against the dragon Nythraxis. An offline single-player mode and a headless reinforcement-learning environment for AI agents share the same game core.
highlights: The playable foundation reportedly took about 2 days, and the open repo has grown to 22,795 commits, 415 PRs, 2.3k stars and 751 forks

One deterministic game core runs in three hosts: the authoritative MMO server, an offline browser single-player world, and a headless RL environment with Python/Gymnasium bindings where seeded episodes replay exactly
Authoritative TypeScript server: clients stream intent at 20 Hz over WebSockets, and characters persist in Postgres 16 as JSONB
Broad content: 9 classes x 3 specs, 6 zones, 7 dungeons, delves, a 10-player raid with voiced dialogue, ranked 1v1/2v2 PvP, 5v5 CTF, professions, guilds, a Dungeon Finder, Card Duel and 22 locales
Art is 'authored in code, not in a 3D editor' (procedural factories plus curated CC0 packs), and the soundtrack is composed procedurally in the repo
story:
According to the developers, Levy Street Games, a Wellington-based AI company, generated the playable foundation over roughly two days in mid-June 2026 using Claude Fable 5. Notebookcheck reports that Anthropic launched that model on 9 June 2026 and suspended access on 12 June. At launch the game had nine classes, three zones and nearly 90 quests. It was open-sourced under MIT, collected thousands of Reddit upvotes, and spread through German tech press (WinFuture, PCGH, PC Games, Notebookcheck), which reported 27,000 to 30,000+ players within days.

Development has continued with other frontier models. The repo ships CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and GEMINI.md plus a Codex operator guide, and now has more than 22,000 commits. v0.12.0 added Nythraxis, the first 10-player raid, with its own questline, music and voiced dialogue, and the live site is now at v0.45.8. In July 2026 a free-to-play Steam page went up while awaiting approval. The project also added a cosmetic-currency store and ties into a $WOC Solana memecoin.

vibeCoding.aiCodeShare: most of it ('built by working alongside Claude rather than writing every line by hand'); PCGH says 'almost exclusively with AI', though art comes largely from asset packs
vibeCoding.buildTime: playable foundation in ~2 days (one weekend, mid-June 2026); continuously updated since, reaching v0.45.8 by Nov 2026
workflow: Weekend sprint with Claude Fable 5 for the base game, then continued on other frontier models after Fable 5 access was suspended
The repo is set up for several coding agents at once: CLAUDE.md, .claude/, AGENTS.md, .codex/, .agents/skills, GEMINI.md and a Codex operator guide
Open source under MIT, which keeps AI-written code legible to outsiders; it accepts community PRs
Vitest suite plus a fully deterministic core (no wall clock or random calls) so behaviour can be replayed and tested
Example of a silent AI-era bug: loot broke for half of a 10-player raid because PARTY_MAX was still hardcoded to 5 from the dungeon code, with no error thrown
Content ships on a regular cadence (zones, then dungeons, then raid) rather than in one big launch

art.notes: The README says models are 'built by procedural factories and a curated asset library rather than hand-sculpted'. Most of what you see is CC0 (KayKit, Quaternius, Kenney, ambientCG, Poly Haven). Class icons come from CraftPix, and store and prestige art was bought or commissioned. Some props, creatures and backdrops are 'our own generated' assets, but the generator isn't named, so they may or may not be AI. Icons come from a 'layered painter'. Terrain and effects are generated at runtime.

audio.notes: The soundtrack is 'composed procedurally in the repo'. Spatial and UI SFX are sampled, some from @jamiecypher under CC BY-NC 4.0, and some interface sounds are self-generated. The raid has music and voiced dialogue, but sources don't say where the voices come from.

tech.notes: The authoritative server handles HTTP and WS and runs the world loop, with Postgres 16 storing characters as JSONB. Clients send intent at 20 Hz. It deploys with Docker Compose on any VPS behind a TLS reverse proxy (Caddy). Electron provides the desktop app and Capacitor the iOS/Android wrappers, and pnpm manages the monorepo. A headless RL mode exposes a documented protocol, and optional non-custodial Solana wallet linking supports the $WOC token.

traction.monetization: Free to play. The WOC Store sells 'Claudium', a one-way cosmetic currency bought with fiat, SOL, USDC or $WOC (paying in WOC gets a discount), for cosmetic weapon skins with no stat boosts. $WOC is a pump.fun fair-launch Solana memecoin with holder badges and daily reward spins. There are also Ko-fi donations and a free-to-play Steam page (wishlist only).
traction.notes: Player numbers come from press and the site counter, not an audited dashboard. Outlets give 27k vs 30k+ and don't say whether that means registered or concurrent players. The live counter didn't render when the site was fetched.

reception: Big viral and press reach, but gamers were not impressed. Many Redditors called it a proof of concept rather than an MMO and flagged scalability, netcode, database structure and security. Experts quoted by WinFuture said parts of the code look unstructured and hard to maintain, and PCGH called the gameplay rough and the intro 'raw'. Some argued it is less 'AI-made' than it seems because it leans on free asset packs. PlayToEarn reported no token-specific controversy around $WOC.
lessons: Scope, not typing speed, is the bottleneck: AI just gets you to the hard design questions sooner (creator)
Silent logic bugs slip through, for example a hardcoded party size of 5 that broke loot in 10-player raids
Generating the code fast doesn't make it a production MMO: scaling, netcode, moderation, security and long-term motivation remain the hard parts
Depending on one model is risky: the model that built the foundation was pulled after 3 days, and work continued on other models
CC0 asset packs make an AI-built world look good fast, but they invite 'not really AI-made' pushback

title: Codex Mortis
tagline: Billed as the world's first 100% AI-made game: Claude Code wrote engine-less TypeScript, ChatGPT drew every sprite, and it hit Steam 1.0.

creator.name: GROLAF
creator.background: Solo developer who built it as an after-hours hobby project; published by CRUNCHFEST (PC Gamer reports he posts online as 'Crunchfest3')

summary: An isometric horde-survivor bullet hell with a roguelite loop built around a spell deckbuilder. You play a necromancer and build a deck from your spell collection before each mission, and souls earned in runs buy booster packs that grow the collection. Version 1.0 has 10 schools of dark magic, 200 spells, a mutation system that changes how spells behave, 31 heroes, 14 levels, split-screen local co-op and online co-op for up to four players.
highlights: No engine: pure TypeScript + PixiJS + bitECS wrapped in Electron, ~350k lines over ~3,450 commits (self-reported)
At launch, character 'animation' was a Claude Code-written shader that sways the still ChatGPT sprites instead of frame-by-frame animation
Steam-hosted online co-op for up to 4, with password lobbies and mid-run rejoin, plus split-screen local co-op
200 spells in 10 schools, and 249 mutations that change spell behaviour (a bone spear becomes a 360° nova); final boss has 3 phases and 600,000 HP
Steam Deck Verified, native Linux build, 28 languages
Demo drew 10,500 players averaging 71-minute sessions (self-reported)
story:
GROLAF started in July 2025 with a Vampire Survivors-style prototype generated in a chat window, to test whether a whole game could be made with AI. Off-the-shelf engines stalled because AI tools struggle with engines built around human GUIs. He asked the AI which language it knew best (JavaScript) and built a custom TypeScript stack, vibe-coded in Claude Code (mostly Opus 4.1 and 4.5 at demo time) on a $200/month Claude Max plan. About three months in, on December 9, 2025, the Steam demo launched under the banner 'world's first fully playable game created 100% through AI'. Its trailers were deliberately obviously AI, and it drew 10,500 players. Early Access followed on March 26, 2026 at $3.99.

Six months of Early Access brought 20+ patches and a lot of rebuilding. Context-length limits broke the original design and forced a move to an ECS core, and roughly 100 bugs traced back to duplicated code paths. In August 2026 the game switched from top-down to isometric, and every character sprite was recreated. Version 1.0 shipped on September 24, 2026 with Steam-hosted online co-op, 100 more spells and 20 more heroes, alongside a ~15-minute documentary about the build. The developer says the project reached ~3,450 commits and 350,000+ lines of TypeScript.

vibeCoding.aiCodeShare: ~100% (marketed as 100% AI-made; Steam disclosure: 'AI is used for entire code of the game, text, arts, sounds and music')
vibeCoding.buildTime: prototype July 2025; demo ~3 months later (Dec 2025); Early Access Mar 2026; 1.0 Sep 2026 (~14 months, after hours)
workflow: Began as a Vampire Survivors-style prototype in a chat window, then moved to Claude Code
Dropped game engines because AI struggles with tools built for human GUIs, asked the AI which language it knew best, and built a custom TypeScript stack around that
'Define the task, delegate it, review the result': the developer kept the core design, theme and worldbuilding himself
An instruction file told the AI the user was frustrated and to skip apologies and explanations; he says it helped
Moved the code onto an ECS (bitECS) after context-length limits broke the original design; he calls AI 'a good programmer' but not a good architect
~100 bugs over months, mostly duplicated code paths where the AI fixed only one copy
Single Claude Max plan ($200/month) with no extra token purchases

art.style: 2D dark-fantasy pixel-style sprites, isometric view (top-down until Aug 2026)
tools: ChatGPT (regular chat, not the image API)
art.notes: All art came from ordinary ChatGPT chats, not the image API. The developer found chat kept his preferred style across sessions best, though a consistent style was still 'difficult'. Frame-by-frame character animation didn't work out, so Claude Code wrote shaders that wobble and sway the still sprites; players called the characters 'still images'. The August 2026 switch to isometric meant recreating every character sprite. A May 2026 press release claims every character and enemy is now fully animated, without saying how.

audio.notes: The Steam AI disclosure covers sounds and music, but the generator(s) are not named.

tech.notes: No engine: TypeScript with PixiJS for 2D rendering, bitECS for the entity-component-system core, and Electron as the desktop shell. Tauri was tried first but 'didn't work well with Steam at all', and Electron's Steam integration 'wasn't as smooth as with Unity or Unreal Engine'. Builds for Windows and native Linux, Steam Deck Verified (Apr 2026). Online co-op runs on Steam hosting with lobbies and rejoin.

metrics.label: Demo peak concurrent players (SteamDB, during a streamer's playthrough)

traction.monetization: Premium: $3.99 (also sold in a bundle with Void Miner)
traction.notes: No sales figures published. The review label has moved over time: 'mixed' at Early Access launch (iXBT, Mar 2026), 'Very Positive, 80%+' (developer press release, May 2026), 'Mostly Positive' (Gaming-ST, Sep 2026) and 'Very Positive, 82% of 102' on the store (Nov 2026).

reception: Fiercely divisive. PC Gamer headlined the demo as 'a milestone for slop everywhere' and questioned the 'world's first' claim, pointing to the ChatGPT-made browser game Doomscroll. Creative Bloq asked whether it was 'the ultimate rage bait'. Steam forum posts included 'Garbage AI slop' and 'Please do not buy or support it', and early players criticised the UI and the unanimated 'still image' characters. The developer says the obviously-AI December trailers were deliberate and argues the backlash is about lazy execution, not the tool: 'We've had asset flips, Unity slop, Unreal slop.' Buyers have been kinder than commenters, at 82% positive across 102 reviews by November 2026.
lessons: Agents work better in a code-only stack they 'know best' than inside GUI-first engines
AI is a good programmer but a poor architect: context limits broke the design and forced an ECS rebuild
Duplicated code paths are the signature AI bug: a fix lands in one copy and not the other
Shipping web tech on Steam hurts: Tauri failed with Steam, and Electron took more work than Unity or Unreal
Consistent AI art is hard, and animation is the weakest link; a shader wobble was the stopgap
'100% AI' marketing buys attention and backlash in equal measure

title: The Great Taxi Assignment
tagline: A GTA: Vice City tribute taxi game built in 65 hours with Cursor and Claude 3.7 Sonnet; won the 2025 Vibe Jam's $10k gold.

creator.name: Tomáš Bencko
creator.background: Frontend developer (React, Vue.js, TypeScript), not a game dev; wrote the build up on the Cassovia Code blog

summary: You drive a taxi through 'Vibe City,' a sun-soaked 80s city inspired by GTA: Vice City, picking up passengers and dropping them across town. Physics-based driving, Miami Vice-style billboards and an AI-generated synthwave soundtrack set the retro mood.
highlights: Physics-based driving on Cannon-es, with simulated gear shifts on a single engine loop and distance-based audio
City blueprint drawn in Adobe Illustrator, imported as SVG, then blocked out with primitives in the Three.js online editor
AI-written two-way converters so levels can round-trip between the game and the Three.js editor
Window placement and random billboard textures handled in code; 80s billboards made with GPT-4o ('Crime has never looked this fabulous')
Original 80s soundtrack generated with Suno and streamed via SoundCloud
story:
Tomáš Bencko is a frontend developer who says game development first drew him to programming. He wanted to test vibe coding by making a scaled-down tribute to GTA: Vice City for Pieter Levels' 2025 jam. He spent 65 hours over about two weeks and roughly €72 on AI services, and submitted on March 31, 2025.

The hardest part was the physics-driven car. Early versions had rotated wheels, cars launching into the air, a chassis lagging behind the wheels, and flips at speed. He restarted from an empty repo four times before the driving model and controls worked, and paused coding for several days just to make music with Suno. The game won 1st place ($10,000) among 1,000+ entries and is still playable.

vibeCoding.aiCodeShare: ≥80% per jam rules; creator didn't give an exact share
vibeCoding.buildTime: 65 hours over ~2 weeks (March 2025)
workflow: Used Cursor's agent mode with Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Gemini 2.5 Pro for multi-file edits
Restarted from an empty repo four times until the driving model and controls felt right
Had the AI write conversion scripts so the map could round-trip between the game and the Three.js editor
Kept a modular, object-oriented Vite codebase so AI edits stayed manageable
Noticed the LLMs layering quick-fix patches instead of fixing root causes; spatial reasoning (axes, orientation, directions) was their weakest area

art.style: low-poly primitive 3D with pixel-art billboard sprites, 80s Miami palette
art.notes: Bencko drew the map as an Illustrator blueprint and placed buildings and objects as primitives (cuboids, cylinders) in the Three.js online editor. Code adds windows and random billboard textures. Billboard backgrounds were generated with GPT-4o and text was added on top; he planned to use Stable Diffusion but dropped it. Palm trees and pedestrians appear as pixel-art sprites, and their source isn't stated.

audio.notes: Music made with Suno (streamed from SoundCloud). Sound effects from ElevenLabs, some tweaked by hand. Volume falls off with distance, and gear shifts are simulated on a single engine loop.

tech.notes: Three.js rendering, Cannon-es physics, Vite build, Netlify hosting, SoundCloud for music streaming. Single-player; the jam listing says not mobile-ready.

traction.monetization: None. Free web game; won the $10,000 prize.
traction.notes: Still live as of 2026-11-24. No player counts published.

reception: Won a 2025 jam judged by a panel that included Andrej Karpathy and Pieter Levels. It shows up regularly in roundups of the best vibe-coded games; Indie Hackers called it a 'GTA-like taxi driver simulator.'
lessons: Vibe coding shines for prototypes, hackathons and 'throwaway' software but struggles with long-term maintainability without experienced oversight
LLMs tend to stack patch on patch instead of fixing root causes
Physics and spatial reasoning (axes, orientation) were the AI's weakest area. Getting car handling right took four full restarts
'What AI still doesn't take over, at least not yet, is responsibility for the result'

title: Counter-Strike Bench
tagline: InstantDB's CTO had GPT-5.1 Codex Max, Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3 Pro each build a multiplayer browser Counter-Strike in ~7 prompts.

creator.name: Stepan Parunashvili
creator.background: co-founder and CTO of InstantDB (a sync database startup); experienced engineer

summary: Three separate Counter-Strike-style browser FPS games, one per model, all built from the same sequence of about seven prompts. Each has a first-person blocky arena with a crosshair, respawning enemies with HP, people and guns made of polygons, a recoiling view-model gun, chiptune shot sounds and death animations. Each also has real-time multiplayer (shared positions, networked shots, death and respawn) and a lobby of five seeded maps that double as rooms. The Claude build won the frontend round; the Gemini and Codex builds are at csgemini.vercel.app and cscodex.vercel.app.
highlights: The same seven-prompt script run on three frontier models, with medals per step: a game-shaped, repeatable coding benchmark.
All three builds are still playable side by side (csclaude, csgemini and cscodex on vercel.app).
Multiplayer with no custom game server: positions go through InstantDB presence, shots through topics, and maps are stored in the database as room IDs with read-only permissions.
All art comes from code. The first prompt says 'Make everything simple polygons -- rectangles', and the models then built people and pistols out of boxes.
Revealing failures: Claude's React useEffect double-mount, Gemini's transparent gun, and Codex calling a function it never imported.
story:
Stepan Parunashvili ran the experiment in the week that Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5.1 Codex Max and Claude Opus 4.5 all shipped, and published 'Codex, Opus, Gemini try to build Counter Strike' on the Instant blog on 2025-11-26, with a video walkthrough. Each model ran on its provider's top-tier plan with the default CLI settings (Codex Max on medium). Each got the same prompts. Four were frontend prompts: boxes and physics in Three.js, enemies that look like people, a POV gun with recoil, and sounds plus death animations. Three were backend prompts using Instant's presence and topics: share positions, network the shots, and add map selection with five seeded maps used as room IDs.

Claude Opus 4.5 took gold in all four frontend steps, with the best map, the most human characters and a gun that 'looks like a real darn pistol'. Gemini 3 Pro won the backend, and Codex landed in between. All three needed errors pasted back during the multiplayer steps. Claude got stuck in a React useEffect double-run that created two canvases, and the team 'had to put our engineer hats on and actually look at the code'. Gigazine, Analytics India Magazine, iXBT and Habr all covered it.

vibeCoding.aiCodeShare: ~100% intended (models built everything from prompts), but a human had to read the code to unblock Claude's refactor
vibeCoding.buildTime: ~7 prompts per model; wall-clock time not stated
workflow: A fixed prompt sequence: boxes + physics, characters, POV gun, sounds/animations, then shared positions, networked shots and multi-map rooms.

Each model ran in its provider's CLI (not named in the essay, but presumably Codex CLI, Claude Code and Gemini CLI) on the highest-tier plan with defaults. The authors credit the CLIs for letting the models iterate on their own work.
Errors were pasted back to the agents in the moving and shooting steps for all three models.
Gemini ran npm run build often, which caught TypeScript errors on its own.
Results were scored with gold, silver and bronze per step across frontend and backend.

art.notes: The prompt asked for simple polygons and rectangles only, for maps, characters and guns. Claude's map had obstacles and a clear floor; Codex's was dark and hard to read.

audio.notes: The prompt asked for chiptune shot sounds; the essay doesn't say how they were produced.

tech.notes: Each build started from Instant's starter app (the page title is still 'Create Instant App') and is deployed on Vercel. InstantDB presence carries player positions, topics carry shots, and maps live in the database with read-only permissions.

traction.monetization: None (published as a showcase on the InstantDB blog)
traction.notes: No player counts. It spread mainly as a benchmark story in tech press.

reception: Covered by Gigazine, Analytics India Magazine ('Counter-Strike becomes the new benchmark for vibe coding'), iXBT Games and Habr. The author's own verdict: the models have improved a lot and handle higher-level feedback, but non-programmers would likely get stuck, and 'The promise that you never have to look at the code doesn't quite feel real yet.'
lessons: The models had different strengths: Opus 4.5 was best at visuals and game feel, Gemini 3 Pro at multiplayer and backend work.
Agents make human-style bugs, such as a React useEffect double-mount creating duplicate canvases, so better dev tooling helps both people and agents.
Multiplayer steps still needed humans to paste errors back; fully hands-off vibe coding wasn't there yet in late 2025.
CLI agents that can run builds and read errors iterate much better than chat-only workflows.

title: Survive the Horde
tagline: A zombie FPS set in Indian villages that Claude Code grew into co-op and battle royale with squads, voice chat and vehicles in 6 weeks.

creator.name: Harsh Kale
creator.background: solo developer; professional background not stated

summary: A browser FPS with three modes. Solo is escalating zombie waves. Co-op is zombie survival with room codes and invite links, and it gets harder as more players join. Battle royale is PUBG/BGMI-style, with a plane drop, freefall, parachutes, a shrinking blue zone, loot, supply drops and bots. The large map is an Indian countryside with named towns, a city called Shivpur, a college campus, a river, farmland and caves. You can drive auto-rickshaws, Thars and tractors and buy gear at roadside shops (dukaans).
highlights: Three modes in one browser game. The battle royale has a plane route, freefall, parachutes, nested zone circles, supply drops, a 'Most Wanted' bounty and red-zone alerts when players start fighting nearby.

Monster AI with sight cones, hearing, scent through walls, packs and pounces (wander -> investigate -> alert -> chase -> search). It uses Quake 2 MD2 models from the three.js examples plus a Sketchfab hellhound and gold dragon.
Squad systems: knock and revive, recall cards redeemed at water towers, team pings, quick chat and opt-in peer-to-peer voice. Bots fill seats, follow you off the plane and revive teammates.
A distinctly Indian setting: chaiwalas, dukaan stalls, auto-rickshaws, Thars, municipal water towers with Devanagari signage, the made-up 'Taara' currency and 'Krunchu Biscuits' heals.
Cheat codes switch the whole room into ink-outline, noir, pencil, ASCII, thermal or 8-bit render styles, or spawn meteors, a black-hole launcher or chain lightning.

Serious performance tooling: a ?perf=1 overlay with p99 and 1%-low frame times plus GPU timer queries, and a headless benchmark with A/B builds. One commit cut physics at spawn from 5.5 to 1.4 ms per frame.
story:
Harsh Kale started the repo on 2026-09-22. A commit titled 'BEFORE CLAUDE IMPL 1' on 2026-10-13 marks the point where Claude Code took over, and 32 of the 76 commits up to 2026-11-22 carry a 'Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5' trailer. Progress came fast. A playable soldier with shooting landed the same day. A co-op WebSocket relay followed on 10-14, hellhounds, a dragon, day/night and weather on 10-15, and a deployable build on 10-16. Two-story houses, crouch/prone, map pins and a phone HUD came days later.

He announced it on the three.js forum on 2026-10-31, without mentioning AI, already with solo, co-op and battle royale modes. November commits added battle royale bots, Duo/Squad teams with knock/revive and WebRTC voice chat, 23 room-wide cheat codes (including a spawnable tank and a flyable bomber), an asteroid event that releases giant snakes and spiders, destructible buildings and a large performance pass. Kale says the project is 'still actively developing'.

vibeCoding.aiCodeShare: unknown; 32 of 76 commits are co-authored by Claude Opus 5.5, and a 'BEFORE CLAUDE IMPL 1' commit marks the hand-off (the forum post doesn't mention AI)
vibeCoding.buildTime: repo started 2026-09-22; Claude Code phase from 2026-10-13; first deployable build 2026-10-16; still updating as of 2026-11-22
workflow: A 407-line, ~18,000-word CLAUDE.md works as a living architecture spec for Claude Code. It covers every subsystem, the network message names, performance rules, asset paths and a scene-tuning workflow.

The CLAUDE.md sets guardrails such as 'Do NOT migrate to React, Next.js, TypeScript, or Babylon.js unless explicitly requested', and keeps the large main.js on purpose: 'modularize incrementally, not all at once'.
Big feature-batch commits co-authored by Claude. For example, one commit added Duo/Squad queues, knock/revive, recall, team talk and voice.

Custom tools for checking AI output: a Mixamo soldier test page that steps through animation blends frame by frame, a Puppeteer headless benchmark with baseline A/B comparison, and an asset-optimization pipeline (gltf-transform, meshoptimizer, sharp).
No test runner is configured. Verification relies on the perf overlay, the benchmark and manual playtesting.

art.notes: Player characters and animations come from Adobe Mixamo. Buildings, gear, creatures and Indian props come from Sketchfab (CC BY, credited in-game). Enterable houses are assembled from Kenney's CC0 Building and Furniture kits, ground textures are Poly Haven CC0 and motorbikes are from Poly Pizza. Most guns, grenades, medkits, cash bundles and biscuit packets are procedural low-poly models built in code. Sketchfab building shells get doorways cut into them by code (Sutherland-Hodgman clipping) and furnished interiors generated inside.

audio.notes: Recorded CC0 samples (~1.2 MB of .ogg, credited in CREDITS.md), packed by a build script. Ambient rain, wind and night drones, plus a heartbeat when hurt. No background music (an earlier horror score was removed).

tech.notes: Three.js r186, cannon-es and Vite with plain-JS ES modules. A 'dumb' Node ws relay handles rooms (up to 8 players in co-op, 100 in battle royale), host election and reconnect/resume. The relay runs on Render because Vercel can't hold WebSockets, and the game itself is on Vercel. The host is authoritative for zombies: it runs the AI and streams 12 Hz monster snapshots, while players stream their own state at 20 Hz. PvP damage is applied by the victim's client. A battle royale match is built from a shared seed. There is a Capacitor 8 Android build and full touch controls. WebRTC voice is opt-in because peer-to-peer connections expose IP addresses.

traction.notes: Very early. The forum launch post had one like, Vercel Web Analytics was added on 2026-11-21, and no player counts have been published.

reception: Little so far. The only forum reply (metin6176) praised the co-op room codes. It advised making hits and zombie state server-authoritative, adding client-side prediction with server reconciliation, rendering remote players ~100 ms in the past and adding server-side lag compensation for hitscan.
lessons: Client-trusted PvP (the shooter reports hits and the victim applies them) is easy to cheat once strangers join a battle royale. The forum advice was to make hits server-authoritative and add lag compensation.
Vercel can't host WebSockets, so the game and the relay are hosted separately (Vercel plus Render).
Asset licensing shapes the repo: raw Mixamo downloads can't be redistributed, so only optimized GLBs are committed, and CC BY credits are shown on the start and pause screens.
Keeping the agent on a leash: a huge CLAUDE.md with explicit 'do not migrate' rules and step-by-step modularization of a monolithic main.js.
Shader errors are invisible in production builds; the docs say to test new shaders with renderer.debug.checkShaderErrors = true.

title: Taipei Rush
tagline: One dev, '200 AIs' and $10k+ in tokens built a GTA-style open-world Taipei for the browser; it claims 1.2M concurrent players in 3 days.

creator.name: aicodewithme (RUSH RUSH STUDIO)
creator.background: Taiwanese indie developer with a day job who built the game after work; Threads is the game's only official account

summary: A free, GTA-style open world set in a low-poly Taipei that runs in desktop and mobile browsers with no download or account. You walk, ride scooters, drive or steal cars, take the MRT and accept missions (93 at launch) on an in-game smartphone. Crimes bring police chases up to a 5-star wanted level, speed cameras photograph you, and running red lights gets you a warning. The story follows a young transplant and A-Ming defending a grandmother's old street from urban redevelopment.
highlights: Dense, recognizable Taipei: Ximending, Taipei Main Station, Taipei 101, the Presidential Office, Longshan Temple, the Shilin and Raohe night markets, NTU and Songshan Cultural Park, plus real road names like Keelung Rd and Fuxing N. Rd

Local-flavour systems: scooters, MRT rides, convenience stores, drink shops and cram schools, speed cameras that snap you, red-light and crosswalk rules, police shouting in Mandarin, lucky-cat collectibles, and an umbrella that opens in the rain
93 missions and a story at launch from a single developer working evenings for about a month
Runs in desktop and mobile browsers with auto-save and a Chinese/English UI; Tom's Hardware found it responsive on an integrated-GPU laptop
Parallel 'AI swarm' development, with a human reconciling conflicting outputs from many models
story:
Taiwanese developer aicodewithme spent about a month of 5–6-hour evenings after a day job orchestrating what they called '200 AIs', which handled everything from researching Taipei road information to writing the game. They announced 'Taipei GTA' on Threads on 28 September 2026, saying they had already spent more than US$10,000 (≈NT$318,000) on AI tokens. Traffic overwhelmed the service on day one, and seeing other players was still 'under development'. On 2 October TVBS reported 1.2 million people playing 'at the same time' within three days, and Tom's Hardware, PCGH and others repeated the number in headlines.

The game has since been renamed TAIPEI RUSH / 臺北狂飆 at the same URL, with no reason given. It is credited to 'RUSH RUSH STUDIO', carries a disclaimer that it is unaffiliated with Rockstar Games and GTA, and the site now links to about ten other 'RUSH' city games. The developer says the Taipei map will keep expanding based on player suggestions.

vibeCoding.aiCodeShare: unknown (presented as AI-built; a human orchestrated the work and reconciled outputs)
vibeCoding.buildTime: ~1 month at 5–6 hours/day after a day job
workflow: Split the work across '200 AIs' / 'hundreds of concurrent AI processes' (self-described, undefined: could be agents, sessions or parallel calls), from road-information research to code
The developer said the hard part was integrating and checking conflicting outputs from multiple AIs
Spent more than US$10,000 on tokens (self-reported, not itemized, excludes labour and hosting)
remio.ai links the developer to AICodeWith, a multi-model API access layer; the specific models aren't disclosed
Shipped fast, fixed the day-one server overload, then iterated on player feedback with map expansion

art.style: low-poly 3D with simple lighting, reminiscent of older GTA games
art.notes: The low-poly city has dense Chinese-language signage on shops and buildings, and street layouts and landmark positions are rearranged for gameplay. Asset provenance (AI-generated, packs or hand-made) is undisclosed, and remio.ai lists it as an open question.

audio.notes: Police shout in Mandarin. 4Gamers reported audio problems in its 2026-09-29 hands-on.

tech.notes: Engine and framework are undisclosed (Three.js not confirmed). It's a static web app on Vercel's CDN with mostly client-side game logic, which keeps server load low. It has quality settings: mobile uses heavier compression, and high settings can cause load and texture problems, so the developer recommends PC.

traction.monetization: Free, with a 'Support' link on the site; no ads or IAP documented.
traction.notes: remio.ai points out that there is no analytics dashboard, hosting report or audited server data behind the number. 'Concurrent' isn't defined (versus visits, sessions or cumulative players), every report traces back to one TVBS interview, and the dates don't line up (the Threads post is dated 28 Sep, TVBS says it launched 1 Oct). A real 1.2M concurrent peak would leave measurable infrastructure traces, although a CDN-served client-side game could absorb heavy traffic.

reception: It went viral in Taiwan and abroad, with coverage from TVBS, 4Gamers, Mirror Media, unwire.hk, a Tom's Hardware hands-on and PCGH. Players praised the local detail. 4Gamers saw black screen areas, long loads on high settings and audio bugs at launch. remio.ai questioned both the 1.2M figure and the 'AI-generated' framing, since a human planned, tested and launched it. Tom's Hardware joked about Rockstar's legal department, and remio.ai flagged brand-confusion risk from the 'GTA' name before the rename.
lessons: Hyper-local settings spread: recognizable landmarks and everyday details drove shares
Big round numbers travel faster than verification: one interview's '1.2M concurrent' was repeated unchecked
Parallel AI agents move the bottleneck to human integration, i.e. reconciling conflicting outputs
Agent-swarm development can cost a solo developer five figures in tokens
Don't put trademarks like 'GTA' in the name; the game has since rebranded
Expect a launch-day overload; static CDN hosting plus client-side logic helps

title: Tower of Time
tagline: A time-rewinding tower defense jam game that was ~95% AI-written, with every prompt published; 319 points on Hacker News.

creator.name: Maciej Trebacz
creator.background: software developer with a full-time day job; Tower of Time was his first ever game

summary: A pixel-art space-station tower defense. You fly a ship around your base, building basic, sniper, slowdown and splash towers against waves of enemies. Building and rewinding both draw on a shared energy pool. The twist is a time-rewind power that lets you roll time back to undo mistakes, but you have to use it sparingly or run out of energy. Supports keyboard and gamepad.
highlights: The rewind mechanic is built on a generic RewindableSprite game object. He ran that prompt through three different LLMs and kept Claude Sonnet 4's version.
He published the full prompt log (PROMPTS.md) and the source, a rare complete record of how an AI-coded game was built.
About 95% of the code was AI-written: 7,667 lines of Cursor Agent edits accepted and 105 Augment Code prompts.
A first-time game maker shipped it for a jam in 25 to 30 hours, gamepad support included.
story:
Maciej Trebacz made Tower of Time, his first game, for Beginner's Jam Summer 2025, a jam for beginners that allowed AI coding and had the theme 'Time Travel'. He worked about 25 to 30 hours over roughly a week, mostly after his day job, and AI agents wrote about 95% of the code. He used Cursor's Agent mode, mostly with Claude Sonnet 4 and occasionally Claude Opus 4 and OpenAI o3, plus Augment Code for multi-file tasks. A teammate, death_unites_us, handled balancing, menu music and testing.

He then published the source and a PROMPTS.md log of his prompts, which he reconstructed from chat history (one count puts it at roughly 130 prompts). His Show HN post, 'I AI-coded a tower defense game and documented the whole process', reached 319 points and started a long argument about how useful AI coding really is.

vibeCoding.aiCodeShare: ~95% (README: 'Approximately 95% of the codebase was written by AI')
vibeCoding.buildTime: 25 to 30 hours over about a week, mostly evenings after a full-time job
workflow: One feature or bug per prompt, attaching the relevant files with @file so the agent had full context.
When Augment Code's agent got stuck on ship inertia (the ship spun randomly), he switched to Cursor with Claude Opus 4 in MAX mode, which fixed it.
Debugging loop: have the agent add console logs, trim the logs that fire every frame, paste real console output and stack traces back in, then have it remove the logs.
When the model misused the Phaser API (tweens, tint), he pasted the relevant Phaser docs into the prompt.
Guardrail prompts such as 'Try not to rewrite everything we have but instead plug into already existing functionality'.
He used Phaser Editor to place level elements visually, and wrote or changed some code by hand.
He used no source control for the first 2 to 3 days, and reconstructed the prompt log from chat history afterwards.

art.notes: Free itch.io assets with slight touch-ups by the author: Space Station by jonik9i, the Ocunid monster by Robocelot, Void Main Ship by Foozle, a pixel gem by Lunarnia and space backgrounds by Screaming Brain Studios. No AI-generated art.

audio.notes: Sound effects come from freesound.org and the menu music is by teammate death_unites_us. The in-game track is 'A - Spacebase DF-9' from Double Fine's Amnesia Fortnight.

tech.notes: Phaser 3.90 with Phaser Editor v4 for prefabs and the level scene, plus TypeScript, Vite and pnpm. HTML5 build on itch.io with keyboard and gamepad input.

traction.monetization: None (free jam game, MIT-licensed source)
traction.notes: The jam ranking isn't shown on the itch.io or GitHub pages.

reception: The Show HN thread became a debate about AI coding itself. Supporters praised the published prompts and said what works is having 'a strong and thorough idea of what you want', broken into smaller problems. Critics said the AI 'wrote probably 5x more functions than it needed' and found the recorded agent sessions slow for one-line fixes. One asked 'at what point is it easier to just write the code?', and another wondered whether the post was an ad for Augment Code. Players reported a tutorial prompt that got stuck and running out of energy early in the game.
lessons: If the AI gets stuck, ask it to add debug/console logs and share the output with the agent (from the README).
Switching tools or models can break a deadlock that re-prompting can't.
Give agents as much file context as possible, and tell them to extend existing code rather than rewrite it.
Use source control from day one. His first commit was huge because he started without it.
AI output tends to be verbose, and some HN reviewers felt the code was over-engineered.

title: WW2 Dogfight Arena
tagline: A multiplayer WW2 dogfight sim made with 0 human code in 20 hours and 500 prompts; its guide became a 4.8k-star vibe-coding playbook.

creator.name: Nicolas Zullo
creator.background: longtime Cursor user (12 months, 3,000+ prompts by his account); game-dev background not stated

summary: A free browser WW2 air-combat game that bills itself as 'the most intuitive free-to-play MMO combat flight sim, 100% made with AI in 500 prompts!' You fly a fighter among the clouds with throttle, boost and fire controls. You can take on AI enemy planes in Solo Mission or join multiplayer Squadron battles.
highlights: A self-imposed rule of zero human-written code: 20 hours, ~500 prompts and ~20 euros of AI spend (self-reported).
The plane is built in code through ~30 targeted prompts guided by a plane-implementation.md spec, for example 'cut out space in the wings for ailerons'.
Audio is synthesized with the Web Audio API (oscillators and generated buffers). A researcher inspection found no sound files referenced in its audio manager.
Plain Three.js ES modules (Three.js 0.152.2 from a CDN) served unbundled, with a native WebSocket multiplayer client and a Vibe Jam portal link.
It started a methodology many others copied: game design document -> tech-stack.md -> implementation-plan.md -> 'memory bank' (progress.md, architecture.md), one step per fresh chat.
story:
In early March 2025, a week after Pieter Levels started the 'make a whole game by prompting' trend with fly.pieter.com, Nicolas Zullo set out to 'humbly try to beat Pieter in terms of look and feel'. He set a hard rule of no human-written code, 'not even a small edit'. By his account it took 20 hours, about 500 prompts and about 20 euros, and his posts drew 1.5M views on X while 45k people tried the game. Hundreds of people asked how he did it, and some offered '(big) money' for his prompts.

On 2025-03-12 he published 'The Ultimate Guide to Vibe Coding Games' for free on GitHub (EnzeD/vibe-coding), and it has reached 4.8k stars. Version 1.0 told readers they only needed 'Grok 3 Thinking' and 'Cursor with Claude Sonnet 3.7 Thinking'. Later revisions moved to Gemini 2.5 Pro and now recommend Claude Opus 4.7 in Claude Code and Codex 5.5, calling Cursor 'less powerful'. The game was entered in Vibe Jam 2025 and is still online, with a sponsor slot on its landing page.

vibeCoding.aiCodeShare: 100% (creator: '0 human code, not even a small edit')
vibeCoding.buildTime: ~20 hours (self-reported), early March 2025
workflow: Grok 3 Thinking wrote the game design document and recommended the stack (Three.js + WebSocket). Claude 3.7 Sonnet Thinking in Cursor wrote the code (Guide V1.0).
Key principle: 'Planning is everything. Do NOT let the AI plan autonomously, or your codebase will become an unmanageable mess.'
implementation-plan.md is a list of small steps, each with a test and no code. The AI keeps progress.md and architecture.md updated as a 'memory bank'.
Work one step at a time: implement, test, commit to Git, start a new chat, repeat. Cursor rules files mark key docs as 'Always' included.
Complex pieces get their own spec file (plane-implementation.md) and sharp, specific prompts rather than vague ones like 'make a plane'.

art.notes: Zullo says 'all assets and code are vibe coded'. The plane was modeled in code over ~30 prompts. His guide recommends Trellis, Tripo or Hunyuan for 3D assets, but it isn't stated that the game used them.

audio.notes: A researcher inspection of the live AudioManager.js (~44 KB) shows AudioContext oscillators and generated buffers and no references to audio files.

tech.notes: Unbundled ES modules (Game, SceneManager, NetworkManager ~100 KB, AudioManager, PlaneFactory, ProtectionZone, QualitySettings), Three.js 0.152.2 from a CDN, a native WebSocket client and Google Analytics. The third-person camera is inferred, not verified: fans praise the player's plane model, which suggests it is visible on screen. A Sorceress Games blog says server capacity was scaled twice in the first ten days (unverified).

metrics.label: Revenue from in-game ad sponsorships (unverified, unattributed)

traction.monetization: Sponsor slot on the landing page (ad sponsorships; ~2K EUR/month in the early weeks per a secondary blog, unverified)
traction.notes: The brief's '~45K players' is confirmed only as Zullo's own claim ('45k tested the game', posted 2025-03-12). No independent figure was found.

reception: One of the breakout games of the March 2025 vibe-coding wave next to fly.pieter.com. Its biggest legacy is the free guide: hundreds of people asked for the prompts, and the repo became a widely copied vibe-coding workflow.
lessons: 'Planning is everything': a detailed design document and an implementation plan of small, testable steps beat ad-hoc prompting.
Detailed models aren't one prompt. The plane took ~30 targeted prompts guided by a dedicated spec file.
Start a fresh chat for each step and keep memory-bank docs current so the AI doesn't lose track of the architecture.
The tools turned over fast. Within about a year the guide moved from Grok 3 + Cursor to Claude Code and Codex CLI, and now calls Cursor 'less powerful'.

creator.background: professional software engineer at Cursor; former Skiff CEO (per a third-party summary)

summary: A free browser city builder in the vein of SimCity 3000/4. You zone residential, commercial and industrial land, lay roads, rail and bridges, place parks and utilities, and watch the city grow. The map is busy with simulated cars, buses, trains, planes, helicopters, boats and barges, pedestrians and emergency services, and you can save several cities. story:
Andrew Milich, who works at Cursor, built IsoCity in Cursor in 'a few days' in December 2025, according to the Russian outlet Shazoo. Shazoo also reports that he generated the building and object sprites with Google's Nano Banana image model. It quotes him (in translation) saying Cursor's built-in browser was a turning point that for the first time combined creativity and programming. vibeCoding.buildTime: First version in 'a few days' (per Shazoo, Dec 2025). 950 commits on main by Nov 2026.
workflow: Built in Cursor. The developer singled out Cursor's in-editor browser, which lets the agent see the running app, as the turning point (Shazoo, translated).

The models used are not disclosed.

The README only says the renderer handles 'both image and canvas sprites', meaning a mix of image files and shapes drawn in code. No first-hand statement from the developer about the art pipeline was found.

tech.notes: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and Lucide icons, with a custom CanvasIsometricGrid renderer. It is front-end only with no backend, and cities are saved locally. Shazoo counted about 450 npm packages and a 4.3 s build. The README mentions no multiplayer.

traction.notes: No player counts found. Press: Shazoo (Dec 2025) and FlowingData (Jan 2026).

In a sim, players notice first when systems look connected but aren't, like police stations that don't affect crime.
Labeling a game 'Made with Cursor' draws anti-AI reactions in some communities, whatever the quality.
A reusable custom engine let one developer spin off a second game (IsoCoaster).

creator.background: Small studio with nine Steam titles (several cozy typing games) that also runs a 'build a game using AI' hosting site. The build story surfaced in a LinkedIn post on the profile of Israel-based game designer Yan Ginzburg; it's unconfirmed whether he wrote it

summary: A 'desktop companion' that lives in a slim strip at the bottom of your screen. Every key you press while working, writing or chatting speeds a hand-drawn steam train past farms, forests and country stations. Between trips you sell cargo where demand is high, collect fares and reinvest in engines, cars, cabooses, station upgrades and routes. story:
nitzan.games LLC released Keypress Express free-to-play on Steam for Windows and macOS on July 17, 2026. The studio is prolific: its Steam support page lists nine titles, including two other typing-themed cozy games (Butterflies & Bloom, Qwerty Garden), and its website pitches a service to 'Build a game using AI'. A self-reported LinkedIn post says the developer described the desktop-companion idea to Claude Code and '973 commits later' it was live on Steam, with no hand-written code. Search found the post on Yan Ginzburg's profile, but the post itself could not be opened. The research brief also reports that Claude swapped the game's rendering layer late in development when the Steam overlay broke it; this could not be independently confirmed.

The launch was followed by a burst of patches: 20 Steam updates between July 31 and September 10, 2026 (27 announcements in all). They covered an economy rebalance, a tutorial that rising car prices had made impossible, a Windows keyboard listener that silently dropped, and the game quitting itself on a 'recoverable graphics hiccup'. They also added graphics startup diagnostics and launch options, a universal macOS build for Intel Macs, fixes for menus stranded on unplugged monitors or other virtual desktops, and new content such as Grain and Mail cars, a mystery caboose draw and Booster Units.

vibeCoding.buildTime: unknown; 973 commits to Steam launch (self-reported), then ~2 months of rapid patches

title: The Librarian 2

creator.name: Matt Wolfe
creator.background: AI-tools YouTuber (FutureTools); not a game developer by trade

summary: A 3D roguelite sequel to The Librarian, a simple 2D vibe-coded browser game. Unruly kids knock books off the shelves, and you race to put them back before the chaos meter hits 100%. The sequel adds procedurally generated library floor plans, power-up drafts, permanent meta-progression, character choices, boss encounters and disasters such as earthquakes and tornadoes inside the library.

story:
Matt Wolfe vibe-coded the original 2D The Librarian about a year earlier (it is still on GitHub). For his August 13, 2026 video 'Making An Actually Fun 3D Game with AI', he tested how far agents had come by asking for a full 3D sequel. He dictated the design through a voice-to-text tool and gave Claude Code (Opus) the original repo. It ran for about 90 minutes and produced a ~10,400-line, 33-module game with zero external asset files, opening it in a browser, taking screenshots and fixing some visual and balance problems on its own.

He then switched to OpenAI's Codex (a GPT-5.6 model) for refinement: bug fixes, balance and feature polish. A markdown design document carried context between the two tools, and GitHub served for backups and restores. Human playtesting drove most of the later fixes. It found reversed movement controls, a meta-progression screen with no back button, a map arrow that ignored facing direction, a pickup bug, a soft lock, enemies so fast they vanished, tornadoes spawning inside buildings, and the player falling 'into nothing'.
